results.summary: This project is a Wokwi-based design that drives a 7-segment display to show even digits. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the exact behavior and implementation are not described. The pin names indicate that the outputs connect directly to the segments of a 7-segment display. No testing procedure or external hardware requirements are documented.

This project is a Wokwi-based design that likely drives a 7-segment display, but the documentation is only placeholder text. The title 'Tutorial4' suggests it may be an educational exercise, but no details are provided. The pin names show outputs for the seven segments and decimal point. Without further documentation, the exact function and testing method cannot be determined.

This digital cipher and interlock system implements a hardware-based safety chain that requires a specific 8-bit input pattern to unlock an output. It uses combinational logic to verify that all subsystems are in the correct state, mimicking a standalone safety relay. The design provides feedback signals from internal gates and can be used as a puzzle demo or as an interlock for machinery. No external hardware is required, and testing involves applying the correct input pattern to activate the output.

This design drives a 7-segment display to show the string 'ykM_1St_CHIP' character by character. It can operate in two modes: a default mode where it cycles through characters based on the clock, and a manual mode where individual characters are selected via BCD inputs. The design requires an external 7-segment LCD for output. Testing involves observing the character sequence or manually selecting characters as described in the documentation.

This project implements the digital backend of a successive approximation register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter, supporting both I2C and parallel bus interfaces. It controls an external capacitor bank and comparator to perform analog-to-digital conversion with selectable 6-bit or 11-bit precision. The design requires external analog components such as an op-amp, precise capacitors, resistors, and MOSFETs. Notable limitations include an undetermined maximum clock speed and the need for external analog frontend circuitry.

This project simulates a German traffic light, with outputs for red, yellow, and green LEDs. The documentation is placeholder text, so the exact sequence and timing are not described. The design likely implements a state machine to cycle through the traffic light phases. No testing procedure or external hardware requirements are documented.

This project implements a 3-bit linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) to generate pseudo-random numbers. The random bits are output on three pins, and additional outputs drive segments of a 7-segment display. The design is a simple digital building block for random number generation. Testing instructions are not provided, but the LFSR can be verified by observing the sequence of bits on the outputs.

This design is an 8-bit ripple-carry adder that adds two bytes and outputs the sum. It is built from one half adder and seven full adders connected in a ripple-carry configuration. The design requires external input devices (such as switches) to set the two input bytes and output devices (such as LEDs) to display the result. Testing involves applying input values and observing the sum on the outputs.

This controller automatically switches the polarity of DC-type model railway turntables to prevent short circuits when rotating along powered tracks. It uses a binary counter and full-bridge control signals to reverse polarity, with error detection if a trigger remains active too long. The design requires external hardware including XOR gates, a full-bridge driver, MOSFETs, and an RC network for the oscillator. Testing involves verifying the counter sequence, polarity switching, and error handling as described in the documentation.

This project implements a hardware lock using a shift register made from flip-flops. The correct 11-bit sequence must be entered serially to activate an output, and a 7-segment display is provided for output. The design requires the user to input bits one at a time with clock pulses. Testing involves entering the correct sequence (10100100010) and verifying that the output turns on.
